7.2.1 Flora

7.2.2 Fauna
Page 7-1
The Bad Creek area is not the only place that the clemsonae variant of the Jordan's salamander is known to occur. The presence of dorsal brassy flecks and white lateral spots are the characters that were once used to distinguish this animal as a distinct subspecies. Dr. Richard Bruce, herpetologist from Western Carolina University, (1967 - see enclosure #3) found that "dorsal brassy flecking and lateral white spotting occur in many escarpment populatious, and the trend of variation is such that drawing geographic boundaries to the subspecies clemsonae and melaventris is impossible (p. 78 of his paper). Be found animals with the Clemson color pattern common in several areas (see Table III of his paper). Dr. Bruce concluded that "on the basis of clinal variation in pigmentation, recognition of the subspecies clemsonae and melaventris is no longer warranted."
Section 7.2.2 has been revised.
Other researchers have studied the entire complex of subspecies in <u>Plethodon jordani</u> over the past 15 years, and have concluded that no subspecies should be recognized (see reports in Enclosure #21 of Supplemental Information of October 8, 1975). Thus, the animal, including all its color variants, is now simply recognized as <u>Plethodon jordani</u>, the Appalachian Woodland Salamander (see Conant, Roger. 1975. A field guide to reptiles and amphibians of eastern and central North American. <u>2nd edition</u>. Houghton Mifflin Co. Boston). The color phase known as the Clemson variant, not only occurs in the Bad Creek area, but also is found in much of the Blue Ridge Escarpment. Because of these findings, we are eliminating some of our original statements on this animal contained in our License Application for Bad Creek Project (Exhibit W, Subsection 2.2.3.1, Amendment 1).
Section 7.2.2 has been revised.
